subject: Ethics & Professional Conduct
title: Co-defendants whose accounts conflict: acting for both (Code 6.2 and 6.5)
scenario: A firm represents Leon Carter and Mason Reid, who are jointly charged with robbery. At first both deny any involvement. In a later private consultation Leon tells the firm that Mason planned the robbery and carried the knife, and that he intends to say so in his defence statement and at trial. Mason maintains a complete denial and has given the firm confidential details of his own account.
stem: Which of the following best describes the firm's position?

options.A: It may continue to act for both, because co-defendants have a substantially common interest in being acquitted.
options.B: It must not continue to act for both; it may continue for one only if it holds no confidential information of the other material to the matter, or the paragraph 6.5 conditions are met; otherwise it must cease acting for both.
options.C: It may continue to act for both if both give informed consent, given or evidenced in writing.
options.D: It may continue to act for both, provided a different fee earner handles each client.
options.E: It must continue to act for Mason, because he instructed the firm first.

explanation: Paragraph 6.2 of the Code prohibits acting where there is a conflict of interest or a significant risk of one, unless the clients have a substantially common interest or are competing for the same objective. Leon now intends to blame Mason, who denies everything. The firm would have to challenge Mason's account for Leon while defending Mason against Leon's allegations. That is a direct conflict, and neither exception applies. The firm cannot continue to act for both. Once it stops acting for one, that person becomes a former client whose confidential information the firm holds. Under para 6.5, the firm may then act for the other, whose interests are adverse, only if effective measures mean there is no real risk of the information being disclosed, or the former client gives informed written consent. Mason has given the firm confidential details of his account, and Leon's information is equally material, so the firm is likely to have to stop acting for both.

why_wrong.A: Their defences are now directly opposed: Leon's defence blames Mason, so there is no strong consensus on how to achieve their aims.
why_wrong.C: Consent is only a condition of a para 6.2 exception, and no exception applies to defendants running defences against each other.
why_wrong.D: Separate fee earners do not create an exception to the conflict; the firm would still be acting for clients with opposing interests.
why_wrong.E: The order of instructions is irrelevant; the question is whether the firm can act for either without misusing the other's confidential information.

key_rule: A firm cannot act for co-defendants whose defences conflict; it may keep one only if it holds no material confidential information of the other or the para 6.5 conditions are met.
authority: SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, paras 6.2, 6.3 and 6.5

subject: Ethics & Professional Conduct
title: Privileged advice mistakenly sent by seller's solicitor: must the buyer be told? (Code 6.4(d))
scenario: Zainab Ali, a solicitor, acts for the buyer of a commercial unit. The seller's solicitors email her a set of replies to enquiries and mistakenly attach a letter of advice from the seller's counsel. The letter discusses a serious flooding risk that is not mentioned in the replies. Zainab realises at once that it is a privileged document that was sent to her by mistake.
stem: Under paragraph 6.4 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, is Zainab obliged to tell her client what the letter says?

options.A: Yes, because she must make her client aware of all information material to the matter of which she has knowledge.
options.B: Yes, but only if the client signs a written waiver of any claim against the seller first.
options.C: No: the duty to make the client aware of all material information does not apply where the information is contained in a privileged document that she knows of only because it was mistakenly disclosed.
options.D: Yes, but only after exchange of contracts, so that the transaction is not disrupted.
options.E: Yes, but she may tell the client orally and must not send the letter itself.

explanation: Paragraph 6.4 of the Code requires a solicitor acting for a client to make the client aware of all information material to the matter of which the solicitor has knowledge, subject to limited exceptions. Paragraph 6.4(d) excludes information 'contained in a privileged document that you have knowledge of only because it has been mistakenly disclosed'. Counsel's advice to the seller is privileged. Zainab knows its contents only because it was attached by mistake, and she realised this at once. So para 6.4 does not oblige her to tell her client what it says. The exception reflects the importance the law attaches to legal professional privilege. In practice she should tell the seller's solicitors about the error and not use the document. She remains free to protect her client by proper means, for example by raising general enquiries and arranging searches and surveys about flood risk, as she would in any commercial purchase.

why_wrong.A: Para 6.4(d) creates an express exception for information in a privileged document known only because it was mistakenly disclosed.
why_wrong.B: No such waiver features in para 6.4; the exception in 6.4(d) applies regardless.
why_wrong.D: The timing is irrelevant; para 6.4(d) means there is no duty to pass on the contents at all.
why_wrong.E: The method of passing on the information does not matter; the 6.4 duty does not arise for this information.

key_rule: The Code duty to tell the client all material information does not extend to information in a privileged document the solicitor knows of only because it was mistakenly disclosed.
authority: SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, para 6.4(d)

subject: Ethics & Professional Conduct
title: Paying an agency for referrals of defendants awaiting trial (Code 5.1(d))
scenario: A criminal defence firm is approached by an agency that offers to refer defendants who have been charged and are awaiting trial in the Crown Court. The firm would pay the agency £100 for each client referred. The agency says the clients would be told about the payment and that the arrangement would be recorded in a written agreement.
stem: May the firm enter into this arrangement?

options.A: Yes, provided each client is told about the payment.
options.B: Yes, provided the arrangement is set out in a written agreement.
options.C: Yes, provided the payments come from the firm's profit costs and not from legal aid funds.
options.D: No, because the firm must not make payments to an introducer in respect of clients who are the subject of criminal proceedings.
options.E: Yes, but only for clients who are paying privately.

explanation: Paragraph 5.1 of the Code regulates referrals and introductions. Generally, clients must be told about any financial interest an introducer has, and any fee sharing agreement must be in writing. Paragraph 5.1(d), however, is an outright prohibition: a solicitor must not receive payments relating to a referral, or make payments to an introducer, in respect of clients who are the subject of criminal proceedings. Defendants who have been charged and are awaiting trial in the Crown Court are clearly the subject of criminal proceedings. The proposed £100 per client would be a payment to an introducer for referring them. Transparency with clients, a written agreement and the source of funding do not matter, because the protections in paras 5.1(a) to (c) apply only to arrangements that are permitted in the first place. Paragraph 7.1(b) of the Code of Conduct for Firms applies the same rule to the firm itself.

why_wrong.A: Telling the client cannot make lawful a payment that para 5.1(d) prohibits outright in criminal cases.
why_wrong.B: A written agreement is required for permitted fee sharing, but it does not authorise a referral payment that is prohibited.
why_wrong.C: The prohibition in para 5.1(d) applies however the payment is funded.
why_wrong.E: Para 5.1(d) covers all clients who are the subject of criminal proceedings, whether privately funded or legally aided.

key_rule: A solicitor or firm must not make or receive referral payments in respect of clients who are the subject of criminal proceedings, whatever disclosure or written terms are offered.
authority: SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs, RFLs and RSLs, para 5.1(d); SRA Code of Conduct for Firms, para 7.1(b)
